title: Compose Named Steps Right to Left
statement:
Write compose(fns). It takes an array of one-argument functions [f1, f2, …, fk] and returns a single function x => f1(f2(…fk(x))). The last function in the array runs first, as in math notation. Composing an empty array gives the identity function, x => x.

The harness passes plain data, so each function is given by name:

  • "inc": x + 1
  • "dec": x − 1
  • "double": 2 · x
  • "neg": −x

The tested entry point is composeRun(names, xs): turn the names into functions, build the composed function once, call it on every value of xs, and return the results in order.

examples.why: double runs first: 3 → 6, then inc: 7. Running left to right would give (3 + 1) · 2 = 8.
No functions: the identity returns every value unchanged.

constraints: 0 ≤ names.length ≤ 200, with at most 20 entries equal to "double"
hints: A function is a value. compose can return a new arrow function that closes over the fns array.
Inside the returned function, which function has to see x first? Walk the array in that order.
Loop from the last index down to 0, feeding each result into the next function, or use reduceRight with x as the starting value.

explain.intuition:
Composition is a pipeline read backwards. compose([f, g, h])(x) means f(g(h(x))), so h touches the value first. The returned function just keeps a running value and pushes it through the array from right to left. Array.prototype.reduceRight does exactly that walk, and an empty array naturally returns the starting value, which is the identity.

This is the same shape as Redux's compose for store enhancers or a chain of higher-order components: withA(withB(Component)). The order matters whenever the steps do not commute, like "add one" and "double".
steps: Map each name to its function.
In composeRun, build the composed function once and map it over xs.
pitfalls: Applying the functions left to right (reduce instead of reduceRight). ["inc", "double"] on 3 gives 8 instead of 7.
Special-casing the empty list with an error or undefined instead of returning the input.
Rebuilding the composition for every input value, which is wasteful when many values share one pipeline.
Nesting closures one per function (the fold version) makes a call stack k frames deep. With thousands of functions that can overflow the stack; the plain loop cannot.

complexity.time: O(k) per call, k = number of functions

solutions.title: reduceRight over the functions
solutions.idea: Start from x and apply the functions from the last to the first.

solutions.title: Fold into one nested function up front
solutions.idea: Combine the functions pairwise into a single function before any value arrives: compose2(f, g) = x => f(g(x)).

followups: Write pipe(fns), which applies the functions left to right. How does it relate to compose?
Every step here is linear, x ↦ a·x + b. How could you collapse the whole pipeline into one such pair so each call is O(1)?
